### The Author to the Reader.

This treatise is deeply personal to its author: and it is only fitting that he who wishes to write about the Cross should also stand beneath the Cross. Should any reader ask why I am writing specifically about the Cross? It is because by writing about the Cross, I hope to lighten the weight of my own cross. Christ performs this work and lightens the burden: He helps us bear even the smallest cross as a shared effort, making it pleasant and eventually crowning it with glory. Therefore, the cross that is received from the hand of the Lord and endured with a willing heart becomes a gentle yoke and a light burden. <note>The author alludes to Matthew 11:30, "For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light," a central theme in devotional literature regarding the transformation of suffering.</note>

> May I never boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world. Galatians 6:14.

> If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. Matthew 16:24.

<summary>In this personal preface, the author explains that his writing serves as a spiritual exercise to help him endure his own suffering. ## Letter to Theophilus.

### I.

It has already been two and a half years, my dear Theophilus <note>The name Theophilus literally means "Lover of God" in Greek; it was often used in pietist literature to address either a specific friend or the "devout reader" in general.</note>, since you requested my opinion regarding the <term>Mystery of the Cross<note>German: *Geheimnis des Kreuzes*. In this context, it refers to the hidden spiritual purpose behind human suffering and the imitation of Christ’s passion.</note></term> within our spiritual correspondence. You wished to encourage yourself in the endurance of your own cross, or that which might meet you on the path of the <term>spiritual life<note>German: *Geistleben*. This refers to the inner development of the soul and one's personal relationship with the divine.</note></term> in which you walk. I am fully convinced, as you are, that to make any progress in this life and to achieve victory over the many enemies who besiege us—or rather, who possess us from within and surround us from without—one must swear an oath to the banner of the cross and have Jesus, the Great Cross-Bearer, as the Captain and Leader of this company.

### II.

At that time, I informed you that I was not in a position to satisfy your wish; and perhaps I never would have been, had the Lord not made me feel His heavy arm through a very long and very heavy cross. Through this, I was indeed outwardly deprived of peace, freedom, and everything that the world calls honor and prestige, but in exchange, I was inwardly [provided] with something else <note>The sentence is interrupted here by the page break; the catchword "ver-" suggests the next word relates to a change or a different state of being.</note>

<summary>The author addresses "Theophilus," reflecting on a request made years prior to explain the spiritual significance of suffering. He notes that he could only write this treatise after experiencing his own period of intense personal trial and loss of social status.</summary>

<keywords>Theophilus, Mystery of the Cross, spiritual life, Jesus as leader, suffering, spiritual warfare, cross-bearer</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>The previous page ended with the catchword "ver-", which is completed here as "versehen" (provided/endowed). This page continues the author's explanation of his personal suffering to Theophilus.</meta>

endowed [with something], all of which surpasses that little bit of outward <term>cross<note>German: *Kreutz*. In pietist terminology, the "cross" refers to the trials, tribulations, and suffering sent by God to purify the believer.</note></term> beyond all comparison. For it is a double-edged sword that separates body and soul, and soul and spirit from one another, through a torment that is indeed painful, yet in its consequences very comforting. I will not cite any specific circumstances to you, neither of the one nor the other; you will anyway have already learned from other persons what has happened to me outwardly, about which each person will have judged according to their narrow or broad, lowly or high insight. For very few among them can perceive God’s purposes and providences with mankind. But as for the internal cross, you will notice some very vivid features of it in several places in this small draft.

### III.

So, to the matter itself: I have experienced the difference between beautiful, profound thoughts and the actual, active practice itself, albeit under constant suffering of the cross. That which one creates through images and imaginations may wound the spirit quite lightly and touch the heart superficially; but that which one feels in the innermost <term>ground of the soul<note>German: *innersten Grund der Seele*. A mystical term referring to the deepest, most essential part of a person where they encounter the Divine.</note></term> is a sword of torment that penetrates through and through. In the chapter on the inner cross, you will see examples of this that are certainly exceedingly painful and sad. The destinies of men are not equal to one another in this regard;

<meta>catchword: each- (German: jedwe-)</meta>

<summary>The author distinguishes between superficial outward trials and the profound "inner cross" that pierces the soul. He argues that true spiritual understanding comes from the lived experience of suffering rather than mere intellectual reflection.</summary>

<keywords>inner cross, spiritual suffering, soul and spirit, providence, ground of the soul, trials, Theophilus</keywords>

--- Page 19 ---
<meta>The previous page ended with the catchword "jedwe-", which is completed here as "jedweder" (each one/everyone). This page continues the author's reflection on the "cross" or spiritual suffering as a form of divine medicine.</meta>

everyone has their little bit of **cross**: the more deep-seated the evil is, the stronger and more bitter is the medicine: the **Great Physician** <note>A common Pietist metaphor for God or Christ, who "prescribes" suffering to heal the soul's corruption.</note> knows what is fitting for our ailments. One must not intentionally bring a **cross** upon oneself, nor wish for one from God; it is enough for us if we make good use of what He sends us. For He alone knows how to measure and prepare it for our salvation: on our part, He requires only a passive and submissive faithfulness, in patience and resignation. The rest will follow in due course.

### IV.

It is easy to talk about contentment in poverty when one lives in abundance; about contempt for the world when one is honored; about patience in sickness, loss, and misfortune when one enjoys constant health, a secure fortune, and the favor of one's benefactors. I, for my part, treasure Job in his loss and on his dung heap, even assuming that he complained somewhat harshly about God’s providence; I commend David’s gentleness while he was persecuted by Saul and by his own son, and cursed by Shimei <note>original: *Simei*. A biblical figure who cursed King David during his flight from Absalom (2 Samuel 16).</note>; I look with pleasure upon the patience of the righteous Tobit <note>original: *Tobias*. The protagonist of the Book of Tobit in the Apocrypha, known for his charity and his patient endurance of blindness.</note> in his blindness; and so forth. Those are true **cross-bearers**!

### V.

If you, therefore, dearest **Theophilus** <note>A Greek name meaning "Lover of God." It may refer to a specific person or serve as a general address to the "god-loving" reader.</note>, [find] anything noteworthy in this small treatise

encounter [anything], or that which bears a mark of the **anointing** <term>anointing (Salbung): In this context, a spiritual feeling or a sense of being touched by the Holy Spirit</term> in itself; then it is to be derived entirely and solely from the source of the All-Good, All-Gracious, and All-Truthful, who is **Jesus** himself. He, although he is the **Lamb** sacrificed from the beginning to the end of time, nevertheless shows himself to all people—sooner or later, for a longer or shorter duration according to the counsel of his wisdom and our needs—either as a young **lion**, who, if not devouring all at once, is certainly gnawing, or as a lion that tears even to the entrails, yes, even gnaws the very bones themselves. 

He is the one who casts man down from his horse, like **Saul** <note>A reference to the conversion of St. Paul (formerly Saul) on the road to Damascus, where he was struck down by a divine light.</note>; who surrounds people from within and without with the terrors of death, like **David**; who brings man to the point where he curses his birthday and complains to **God** that He allowed him to be born, as **Job** is an example. 

In short: he tears down, breaks, and clears out of the way everything that opposes Him, until one entirely abandons oneself to his judgment, his condemnation, and his strict justice. Then he removes his mask and lets himself be seen in his true form: namely, as the **passionate lover of mankind**, toward whom he does not prove himself a lion except to turn them into lambs, and thereafter to let them taste the delights of his love in full measure, after he has first [led them] into the sorrowful desert and the unknown land of their **Nothingness** <note>original: *Nichts*. In mystical theology, "Nothingness" refers to the state of total humility and self-denial where a person realizes they are nothing without God, which is the necessary state for spiritual rebirth.</note>.

### VI.
The writing style of this little work will certainly seem somewhat rhetorical to you; but you must forgive the author, given his situation. After enduring more than eight months in prison without paper, pen, or ink, he finally enjoyed the pleasure, upon his release, of committing to paper his thoughts on the **Mystery of the Cross** <term>Mystery of the Cross (Geheimniß des Kreuzes): A central mystical concept referring to the spiritual necessity of suffering and the "death of the self" to achieve union with the divine.</term>, and other ideas with which he had long been pregnant. To some extent, for the calming and encouragement of his spirit and soul, he made use of whatever writing style immediately presented itself, without specific choice or scrutiny. These thoughts flowed onto the paper of their own accord, without effort and without much reflection; it is a work of as many days as you will find chapters here, and produced in only as many hours of the day as a man of my age, who writes quite slowly, requires for such a task.

### VII.
I must confess myself that you will encounter certain passages within it that are somewhat difficult to understand. For it is the "birth" of an old man in prison <note>original: "Geburt eines Alten im Gefängnisse." While the author mentions being released in the previous paragraph, he views the book as the intellectual offspring of his time in captivity.</note>, who no longer enjoys the freedom of a lively and cheerful youth. In exchange, however, you will perhaps find therein a more "digested," richer, and more mature nourishment than you would from a younger author. For indeed, very **magical** <term>magical (magisch): In the context of 17th and 18th-century mysticism, "magical" refers to the hidden, supernatural power of the divine working through nature or language to transform the soul.</term> passages occur

<summary>The author explains that the book's spontaneous and rhetorical style resulted from his sudden release after eight months of imprisonment without writing materials. He positions the work as a product of his old age and suffering, offering "mature nourishment" and mystical insights despite its occasional difficulty.</summary>
<keywords>Mystery of the Cross, imprisonment, spiritual maturity, writing style, mystical theology, old age</keywords>

### VIII.
Certain matters known to you are, of course, not dealt with entirely thoroughly here; however, here and there you will encounter certain footprints that lead to a broad trail toward the fundamental truth; but these will only be recognizable to those who have good telescopes <term>telescopes (Ferngläser): Used here metaphorically for spiritual discernment or deep intellectual insight.</term>. For, even assuming that I might be somewhat obscure, I did not wish to explain myself more clearly, so that the reader might also have some practice in reflection and investigation.

### IX.
I have, moreover, well noticed that the French language is too soft and delicate for such vividly penetrating and touching subject matter, and that it has neither the emphasis nor the spiritual depth <note>original: "das Geistreiche," suggesting a mix of wit, intellect, and spiritual essence.</note> of the Latin and German languages. But since most of our friends do not understand these languages, I have sought to satisfy them in the one they are familiar with; and I pray to the Spirit of Grace and Anointing <term>Spirit of Grace and Anointing (Geist der Gnade und der Salbung): A theological reference to the Holy Spirit’s role in providing divine wisdom and internal teaching to the believer.</term> that He, through His power and enlightenment, might come to the aid of my weakness and ignorance, and [fill] the lack...

### X.
I commend you, beloved Theophilus <term>Theophilus: Derived from Greek, meaning "friend of God." ### To the Reader.

To recount the entire story, or all the circumstances that gave rise to this little treatise, there is neither the time nor the place here. However, this might perhaps happen in the future in a separate, very brief and moving piece of writing; if it were the will of the Most High <note>original: "des Höchsten," a common title for God</note>, who calls all his obedient creatures to Himself and leads them along paths that are pleasant and adverse, level and bumpy, overgrown with roses and with thorns, just as it accords with His pleasure and our needs. Consequently, these paths are inscrutable to human reason and wisdom, which is entirely blind and foolish in regard to God's ways.

## Chapter Three.
### Of the Benefit of the Cross.

---

->I.<-

The Cross of Jesus has, from the beginning of the world and continuing until the end of time, established the distinction between two churches: one of which is built upon Mount Zion <note>In biblical tradition, Mount Zion represents the city of God and the dwelling place of the faithful.</note> for the children of God; the other, however, is built in the depths of hell for the children of the devil. The former has constantly been the victim of the latter, and the latter has been the murderer of the former—if not always in effect, then at least in intention. Abel was murdered by Cain. Noah, the priest of righteousness, became a target of sport and mockery for the unrighteous. The father of the faithful, Abraham, received a command from God to leave his land and his kindred <note>The original German "Freundschaft" here refers to one's extended family or kin, a common usage in older German dialects.</note> and to dwell as a pilgrim among an idolatrous people who caused him to endure enough fear and mortal danger. His son, Isaac, was meant to be sacrificed by his own father, even though he was the only son and had been declared the heir of his father's goods and the divine promises of blessing. XI, 29. **True humility of heart** receives and bears every cross willingly and gladly, just as it comes from the hand of **GOD**; it regards the cross as a precious pledge of His care, His faithfulness, and His love, and as the means and sources through which He certainly intends to share new evidence of His grace with us—once He has prepared us through the <term>purification of the cross (Kreuzesreinigung): a spiritual concept where suffering is seen as a refining fire that cleanses the soul of ego and worldly desires.</term>, which increasingly detaches us from ourselves and from earthly things. 

To a soul that is humble of heart, provided she remains faithful, the cross never arrives at an inconvenient time: she immediately bows her neck to have it placed upon her; in lowliness and patience, she opens her arms to embrace it, without first investigating whether it perhaps comes from other people, whether she is being treated justly or unjustly, or whether the burden will be heavy or light, or of a long or short duration. It is enough for her to be certain that it comes, without fail, at **GOD’s** prompting, whose will and pleasure she seeks solely and alone to fulfill, regardless of whatever means He chooses to use to lay the burden upon her. 

This **gentleness** and **humility of heart** always grant the cross-bearer an inner peace, so that he does not grumble, nor become impatient or confused under the weight of the cross. In this way, the fruit of the cross is patience. <note>This section draws on the logic of Romans 5:3, "suffering produces endurance."</note> Tribulation brings patience; the fruit of patience is gentleness and humility of heart.

### Of the Foolishness of the Cross.

### I.

The worldly-wise <note>original: *Weltweisen*. The three main sects <note>Referring to the three state-recognized denominations of the time: Roman Catholic, Lutheran, and Reformed (Calvinist).</note> of Christianity have made, and still do make, an idol <note>original: *Abgott*.</note> out of it, which they consult for advice in doubtful cases, presenting its decisions as divine oracles with proud conceit, and subjecting all other people—who are blindly led by those who are themselves blind—to its laws and ordinances. ### IX.

We are not yet finished here; we must go further and follow our guide step by step; through his wisdom, he will increasingly confirm the **foolishness of the Cross** <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 1:18, where the message of the Gospel is described as "foolishness to those who are perishing."</note>. The greatest elevation in the deepest humiliation! "I thank you, Heavenly Father," said **JEsus Christus** in this state of deepest humiliation, "that you have hidden these high mysteries from the wise and clever, and revealed <note>original: "offenba-" / "offenbart"</note> them to the little ones, the lowly, and the children of the Cross..."

We have previously looked at one side of the commemorative medal of the Cross; now we wish to examine the other, so that we may also become acquainted with its reverse, or opposite side. <note>The author uses the metaphor of a "Schaumünze" (a commemorative medal or coin) to show that the Cross has two "faces": one seen by the world as failure, and one seen by God as victory.</note> It is not unusual for the Holy Scripture, regarding these mysteries, to place before our eyes very specific, inscrutable propositions that seem to be entirely contrary to one another. However, He who commands the light to shine forth from the darkness, who bids life to emerge from death, who calls into being that which is not out of nothingness, and brings back to nothing that which is, so that it may no longer be—He also knows how to unite these wonderful propositions with one another and how to distinguish them. We have seen in the preceding chapter that the Cross is the greatest folly <note>original: "Thorheit" — translated as foolishness, absurdity, or nonsense in a worldly context</note> in the eyes of flesh and blood <note>A biblical idiom referring to human nature or a purely worldly perspective without divine inspiration</note>; now we want to learn to see how it is the highest wisdom in the eyes of God and His children.

### IV.

From these conclusions, we already sufficiently recognize the nobility of the Cross in general; however, I must delve further into specific circumstances to be properly convinced of the majesty and sublimity of its wisdom, which will incite us to endure it with all the greater joy. That which the self-existent Word of the Father—the eternal Wisdom, the source of all light and all life, in which all treasures of heavenly and earthly sciences and knowledge lie locked away—has chosen and loved as a most excellent instrument, must certainly and necessarily be the highest wisdom.

### IV.

**God**, who is truthful in His words and faithful in His promises, sees everything that happens in the utmost secrecy. To such a heart—plagued by <term>restlessness of the soul</term> <note>original: *Gemüthsunruhe*; a state of spiritual anxiety or agitation often seen in Pietist literature as a precursor to conversion.</note> and contrite, cast down out of **humility**, and laden with the vivid feeling of its misery and pain—He has promised through the prophet **Isaiah 57:15**: that He does not remain and dwell with hearts that are completely unrestrained in joy and delight, but with those who are of a broken heart and a humble spirit, who are the **true sacrifice** <note>A reference to Psalm 51:17, "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart."</note> whose scent is pleasing to Him. 

The **Lord** is near, says the **Psalmist** in **34:19**, to those who are of a broken heart, and helps those who have a crushed spirit. Thus, the **Lord** finally allows Himself to be found through persistent seeking, through constant prayer, and through the intense and unceasing knocking of the faithful and troubled soul. To her, He not only offers a tiny drop of His **living water** to quench her parched thirst, but also reveals to her the riches of His **glory**, and little by little imparts the gifts of His Spirit—if only she embraces Him with the arms of her burning desire and holds Him fast with the bonds of her love and faithfulness, despising everything else, in order to [serve] only Him...

### VIII.

the Lord usually behaves toward those under His care like hunters toward a stag <note>The stag is a traditional symbol for the soul in Christian mysticism, often drawn from Psalm 42: "As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul pants for you, my God."</note> that they have driven into a deer park: after they have let it be chased back and forth and worn down long enough by the dogs released and set upon it, they call the dogs back to allow the stag time for recovery and refreshment. The stag now believes itself to be safe and to have nothing more to fear; it recovers, regaining new strength and power through its grazing; one moment it walks here and there, the next it rests again. Finally, when it believes all its danger is over, the hunters—contrary to its expectations—suddenly release their dogs upon it once more, letting them attack and hunt it with force. The dogs pursue it with all the more heat and eagerness, the more strength it shows in trying to escape them. After this, it is allowed to rest once more, only to be attacked again in a new hunt. 

The conduct of God toward souls is very often much the same, because of their fundamental and hopeless corruption <note>This reflects a Pietist view of "total depravity," suggesting that human nature is so deeply flawed that it requires repeated "shaking" by God to be purified.</note>, until they become daily more and more established in the ways of the Lord, until they are adorned with His grace, clothed with His gifts, and filled with His knowledge through the foretaste of the Word of Life and the powers of the coming age <note>original: *Kräfte der künftigen Zeit*; this is a direct reference to Hebrews 6:5, describing a mystical experience of heaven while still on earth.</note>.

Nothing is more contrary to that light than self-exaltation or spiritual pride, which occurs when the "All" <note>In mystical theology, "The All" refers to God's plenitude, while "The Nothing" refers to the human condition without divine grace</note> withdraws from the "Nothing," as we see in the case of **Lucifer** and his companions.

### XII. 

The proper manner of one’s conduct in this situation is this: that one must suffer and be still for as long as it shall please the Lord. *In being still and in hoping shall we be strong.* <note>Isaiah 30:15; in contemporary Bibles often rendered as "In quietness and in confidence shall be your strength"</note> For however hidden the Lord [may remain...]

## XIII.

This is the **highest school** in which one learns that **God** alone is the highest and only Good; that we are but shadows, ash, and dust—indeed, nothingness itself before Him; that He may indeed plague us, but does not cast us off forever; rather, according to His great mercy, He has compassion (**Lamentations 3:31–33**); that, though He may hide Himself, He nevertheless remembers us in His heart (**Job 10:13**); that one must suffer this because the right hand of the **Lord** can change all things (**Psalm 77:11**); and that one must bear **God’s** wrath because one has sinned against Him, until one may once again see delight in His grace (**Micah 7:9**). 

The assurance of divine grace must therefore be sufficient for us, just as it was for the **Apostle** when he was disciplined by the **angel of Satan** <note>A reference to the "thorn in the flesh" mentioned by the Apostle Paul in 2 Corinthians 12:7–9; despite his suffering, he was told "My grace is sufficient for you."</note>. It is in this very **furnace** that the <term>chosen</term> <note>The "elect" or those specifically called by God to a deeper spiritual path</note> are tested and purified to the highest degree. This is also a state in which no <term>creature</term> <note>In this context, "creature" refers to any created being or thing—such as friends, family, or worldly distractions—as opposed to the Creator</note> can provide either comfort or help; and it would be not only a weakness, but also a very great infidelity toward the soul, if one were to reveal one's state to any creature or complain to them of one's suffering. The only exception would be if **God** specifically sent one of His friends to the soul—someone who is, consequently, more enlightened and sincere than **Job’s friends** <note>In the Book of Job, his friends initially came to comfort him but ended up falsely accusing him of sin</note>—to comfort and strengthen the soul in its suffering. For only He who has led the soul into this state can lead it out again...

<summary>This page describes spiritual suffering as a "highest school" where the soul learns total dependence on God and the necessity of divine purification. It cautions the believer to seek comfort only in God's grace rather than from other people or "creatures."</summary>

### III. 

Let us allow ourselves to be led by faith to a person sighing under the burden of the cross <note>The "burden of the cross" is a traditional Christian metaphor representing the trials, sufferings, and spiritual duties a believer must carry in life.</note>, who lies stretched out upon his bed with a dangerous illness that threatens him with imminent death. # Chapter Eight.
## Of the Use of the Cross.

->I.<-

To make good use of a thing, one must know what it is in its own self, in its essence, where it comes from, for what it is intended, and toward what it is directed. We have seen in various places what the cross <term>Cross (Kreuz): used here not just as the physical object of the crucifixion, but as a metaphor for the trials, suffering, and spiritual burdens of a believer</term> is in and of itself, and what the wonderful mysteries are that it contains within itself. Every small cross of man is, as parts of the whole, taken from the great cross of Jesus. According to this great pattern, it is sent, ordained, and proportionately measured out by divine wisdom, which distributes and allocates it according to each person’s need and capacity.

Jesus knew what kind of death he had to die; he knew that this bitter cup <note>A reference to the "cup of suffering" mentioned during Jesus's agony in the Garden of Gethsemane (Matthew 26:39).</note> was intended and sent to him by his eternal Father; he knew that his hour had come, when the hour of the power of darkness was at hand. ### VIII.

All suffering <note>original: "Alles sein Kreuß," literally "all his cross." In this context, "cross" is a standard Pietist metaphor for the personal trials and tribulations God ordains for an individual.</note> is ordained for this purpose: that we should take our refuge in the fountain of grace and divine mercy. Without being visited by the cross, and without the reminder it provides, we would spend our lives in total forgetfulness of God and in the neglect of our duties toward Him.

If, on the other hand, we are plagued by bodily pain or spiritual anguish, or see our hopes frustrated; if we are deprived of our friends, our wealth, or our honor, or are otherwise disturbed in our carnal rest <note>original: "Fleischesruhe." This refers to a state of worldly comfort where the "flesh" (the fallen human nature) feels secure and satisfied, often leading to spiritual lethargy.</note>; and if we can no longer find help, counsel, or any means of deliverance among created things, nor find refuge and support in our own rationalizing, worldly cleverness <note>original: "vernünftelnden fleischlichen Klugheit." Isaiah expressed this very beautifully in chapter 26, verse 16: "Lord," he says, "when distress is present, they seek You; when You discipline them, they cry out in their anxiety." <note>Isaiah 26:16. The author uses a Lutheran translation style common in the 18th century.</note>

A technical term in mystical and Pietist literature referring to the practice of withdrawing one's senses and thoughts from the world to focus on the internal presence of God.</note>, withdraw from external turmoil and internal unrest. ### On the Misuse of the Cross, and especially the Cross of Jesus.

->I.<-

The **natural man** <note>original: "Der natürliche Mensch." If he encounters any—as must inevitably happen—he becomes angry, impatient, and surly; he takes it out on the creatures <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to fellow human beings or external circumstances that the person blames for their misfortune.</note> whom he regards as the cause of his misfortune, turning pale and trembling with rage like an unrestrained animal that refuses to submit to the yoke being placed upon it. # Chapter Ten.
## On God’s Intentions in the Cross.
<note>In this context, "the cross" (*das Kreuze*) refers to the trials, tribulations, and suffering that a believer undergoes as a means of spiritual discipline and refinement.</note>

---

->I.<-

God’s intention in the creation of man was to allow a living impression of His image—along with all His divine attributes—to shine within him: in his soul, in his understanding, and in his will. Indeed, He intended for man to reflect all His divine powers in his entire conduct, namely pure holiness, righteousness, and goodness. This was so that He might take His pleasure in man and make him eternally blessed in every way and in everything that constitutes a human being. To this end, He imprinted the image of His divine wisdom into his understanding; the image of His righteousness, His kindness <term>kindness: the original *Leutseligkeit* implies a gracious, approachable, and philanthropic nature</term>, and gentleness into his spirit; and the image of His fervent love and mercy into the inclinations of his heart. He did this so that nothing might be lacking in the complete and perfect representation of the divine powers and attributes in man, who lived before God in great purity, simplicity <term>simplicity: *Einfalt* refers here to a state of being "undivided" or "guileless" in one's devotion to God</term>, and innocence. He left him in perfect submission and obedience

The Cross is therefore, according to God’s decree <note>original: *Rathschluß*; refers to God's eternal plan or divine counsel</note>, the only true means for the purification of the impure, for the restoration of the New from the Old, and for the reconciliation of all enmity, adversity, and all strife. VIII. ## Eleventh Chapter.
### Concerning the Cross after Death.

->I.<-

Up until now, I have spoken of the cross as a light burden that is laid upon us throughout this life. I must now also speak of that cross which accompanies our souls after this life, which will be far heavier and of longer duration if we have neglected the favorable time and the days of salvation that the Lord granted us while we still enjoy the outward light <note>The "outward light" refers to the period of physical life on Earth, as opposed to the spiritual reality of the afterlife.</note>. # Chapter Thirteen.
## On the Wonders of the Cross in Outer Nature.

---

->I.<-

The more physical things remove themselves from unity—or from their central point—the more they expand into diversity, multiplicity, and divisibility. By contrast, the center point from which they originated remains eternally the same, unique, and inseparably at one with itself, as it constantly draws the surrounding circumference toward itself. For the center point concentrates and contracts, while the circumference widens and expands. 

Created beings, therefore, as they move away from their center, also move away from their power, their influence, and their <term>inner radiance</term> <note>original German: *Einstralung*. In mystical philosophy, this refers to the divine light or energy that flows from the Creator into and between all living things.</note> into one another. Consequently, they become much weaker, more helpless, and more antagonistic toward one another due to the diversity that multiplicity entails. Yet, within this diversity caused by multiplicity, the wonders of unity still appear; for unity would not be manifest if it did not communicate itself through multiplicity <note>The German text ends mid-word with "mittheilg," which—combined with the catchword "theilg"—suggests the word "mittheilte" (communicated/imparted). The sentence likely concludes on the next page.</note>

It establishes the "Center" as a point of absolute unity and power that continually seeks to draw all things back to itself.</summary>

### VIII.

The entire life of **JESUS** is nothing other than a simple, interconnected tapestry of this humbling cross. At one moment he is despised as a worthless fellow among the common folk, and out of contempt called the **carpenter's son**; at another he is treated as a deceiver of the people. On other occasions he is regarded as a glutton, as a friend of sinners and tax collectors. Another time he is held to be an <term>energumen</term> <note>original: *Energumen*; a term derived from Greek used to describe someone possessed by a demon or evil spirit.</note>, or one possessed by the devil. Here they want to stone him; and there, cast him down from the mountain. Are these not nothing but contradictory and conflicting things? On one hand they want to make him king; and on the other they treat him as the lowest slave, whom they trample underfoot like an earthworm. He has nowhere to lay his head to rest. Neither he nor his followers possess anything of their own; so much so that, in order to pay the tax <note>Referring to the half-shekel Temple tax; according to Matthew 17, Jesus provided the coin via a miracle involving a fish.</note>—which he did not even owe—he had to perform a miracle. To support the work of his Father, he chooses a company consisting entirely of common, ignorant, and even unteachable people; whose coarseness, ignorance, and stubbornness he endures with a **patience**, **gentleness**, and **humility** that has no equal. His good deeds are rewarded with ingratitude. His teaching is decried as deception. His prophetic spirit is mocked and blasphemed.

### XI.

The entire teaching of **Jesus** had no other ultimate purpose than the command and the recommendation of the cross. He came to bring the sword into the world, and not peace! If anyone wishes to be his disciple, he must deny himself, die to the life of the "old man" <term>The "old man" (German: "alte Mensch") is a biblical concept referring to the sinful, worldly nature of a person before spiritual rebirth.</term>, carry his cross daily and without ceasing, and follow him in every state—of suffering, of mortification <term>original: "Tödtung." In this context, it refers to the spiritual practice of "killing" one's own ego and worldly desires.</term>, and of death—into which it may please Him to place him for his testing and purification. 

The one who seeks to preserve his natural life by following his appetites and desires, and who is unwilling to exert the necessary force upon himself—which the kingdom of heaven absolutely and without exception requires in order to die to everything that is not of **God** and His will—that person will lose it. However, the one who loses it through generous self-denial and through contempt for all that the world offers: health, beauty, goods, honor and reputation, benevolence, friendship, comfort, or even the outward and physical life itself; that person shall preserve it for the sake of eternal life. And just as great a loss as he has suffered here, so great a gain will he find again there, with very great interest; a hundredfold...

### XII.

If the entire teaching of **Jesus** is focused solely on the cross, then his whole life is simply the practice of it; namely: not to do his own will, not to seek his own honor nor his own pleasure; *Christus non sibi placuit* <note>original: "Christ did not please himself." This refers to Romans 15:3, emphasizing Christ's self-denial.</note>: to constantly die away from the sinful nature with which he was clothed, to let himself be filled with shame, and to be given gall to drink. <note>Gall was a bitter substance (possibly bile or wormwood) offered to Jesus during the crucifixion; it symbolizes the height of his suffering and humiliation.</note> 

Herein lies his unceasing practice: to do good to everyone, and to receive nothing but ingratitude as a reward; as **Lord** and Master, to serve his servants; as King, to wash the feet of his subjects; as Lawgiver, to subject himself to the law in all things; to have daily interaction with the poor, and to proclaim the Gospel to them—*pauperes euangelizantur* <note>original: "the poor have the Good News preached to them." Matthew 11:5.</note>—because they are more inclined to accept and practice it than the rich and powerful, before whom **Jesus** remained silent: *Jesus autem tacebat* <note>original: "But Jesus remained silent." ### XIII.

What makes the yoke of his humiliating cross far heavier and more unbearable for anyone else than for him, is the consideration: by whom, for whom, and why he bears it and suffers.

1. From whom does it come? # Chapter Fifteen.
### Of the Victorious and Triumphant Cross
### of JESUS Christ.

---

->I.<-

The last words of Jesus Christ on his humbling cross, "it is finished" <note>original Latin: *consummatum est*</note>, are the foundational and principal proof of his victorious and triumphant cross. Nature itself may tremble with terror, the rocks may split, the curtain in the temple may tear, the sun—this visible point of the inner light in the heavens—may withdraw its light and grow dark, the angels of peace may weep bitterly, and all of heaven and every creature may be in mourning because of the suffering and death of Jesus; meanwhile, we wish to accompany his spirit into the dark dungeons <note>This refers to the "Harrowing of Hell," a traditional Christian belief that between his Crucifixion and Resurrection, Christ descended into the realm of the dead (Limbo) to liberate the souls of the righteous who died before his coming.</note> into which he descends; in order to bring there the light of the Gospel <term>Evangelium</term> and the good news of the salvation won for the entire human race, and thus also the news of the defeat of all his enemies. What an ecstasy of joy for all the patriarchs, prophets, and other holy souls of the Old Covenant <term>Old Testament</term> who for centuries had been wait- <meta>catchword: waiting (warteten)</meta>

## To the Reader.

Reading these verses of mine, if you bring a chilly heart:
->These verses will be cold to your heart.<-
But if you truly have a loving heart: you will glow, you will grow warm from the fire
->By which my muse is warmed, by which my love burns.<-

### The Bird in the Cage.
<note>This is a common mystical metaphor where the bird represents the soul and the cage represents the physical body or the constraints of earthly life.</note>

->The bird sings of the Master’s care and gifts within the cage.<-

### II.
### The Transforming Stone.
<note>The "Transforming Stone" refers to the Philosopher's Stone of alchemy, which practitioners believed could turn lead into gold. Here, the author uses it as a metaphor for spiritual transformation through Christ or Wisdom.</note>

You lead me to the *Stone of the Sun*, O Virgin Wisdom:
<note>original: *Sophia*. In mystical tradition, Sophia is the personification of Divine Wisdom.</note>
->For this is how you are truly accustomed to play with your disciples:<-

<note>original: *Sophorum*. This refers to the "Sophists" or the worldly philosophers and alchemists.</note>
->To me, you are the Moon-making and Sun-making Stone.<-

### XXXIX.
### The Silkworm
### a symbol of solitude and resurrection.

God, who clothes the little worm with wings, can also

### XL.
### The Slave and the Freedman.
When I, though born free, serve my sins: I am made

### XLIII.
### Eve and Ave.
<note>This refers to the "Eva/Ave" palindrome. In medieval theology, the name of Eve (EVA) was seen as the reverse of the Angel Gabriel’s greeting to the Virgin Mary (AVE). This symbolized Mary reversing the "sin of Eve."</note>

->EVE the parent portends death, and AVE salvation:<-
->EVE destroyed mankind, whom AVE restored!<-

### XLIV.

->The learned and the unlearned! Great men and dwarves: the powerful,<-

### XLV.
### The Idea of an Idea.
<note>original: *Idea ideae*. This poem explores the Platonic and Neoplatonic concept of "Ideas" or archetypes—the perfect mental forms that exist before a physical thing is created.</note>

<note>The poet describes the "Idea" as a self-generating mental process where the thought creates the form, and the form defines the thought.</note>

->tender,<-
->Bright: and a gentle image of the conceived thing.<-

### XLIX.
## Absalom Hanging.
->*2 Samuel XVIII, 9. 14.*<-

### L.
## The Author’s Triple Cross.
<note>original: *Crux trina Autoris*. The "cross" here serves as a metaphor for personal suffering or "burdens to bear."</note>
The first cross was once imposed by a blind clergy,
falsely accusing two brothers in doctrine.
The second came to me from a puffed-up **Sophist**:
<note>original: *Sophista*. In this context, it refers to a deceptive or pedantic scholar who uses clever but false arguments.</note>

The third was devised by a hated **Iscariot**;
<note>original: *Ischariote*. A reference to Judas Iscariot, signifying a personal betrayal by someone close.</note>
whose reason I do not yet know: perhaps I shall.
These are external: but that which God added
within;
Far surpasses all other crosses: a cross both { **blessed**, / **burdensome**, }

---

### LI.
## The Great Climacteric Year 63.
<note>In early modern thought, the "Climacteric Year" (usually multiples of 7 or 9) was believed to be a critical turning point in a person's life. The 63rd year (7 x 9) was considered the most dangerous "Grand Climacteric."</note>
This age denotes, as it is said, a thousand perils:
And it portends many evils, and nothing of good.
The prophet who records these things reached such an
year:
->In which my liberty, name, and honor<-
->perish.<-
Yet many gifts this year simultaneously promises me:
->In which my liberty, name, and honor<-
->return.<-
<note>The author suggests that while his 63rd year brought about the destruction of his reputation and freedom, it also holds the mystical promise of spiritual or social restoration.</note>

### LII.

->**The corruption of one is the generation of another.**<-
<note>original: *Unius corruptio, alterius generatio.* A classic Aristotelian and alchemical principle stating that nothing is truly destroyed, only transformed into something else.</note>
What cruel winter destroys, gentle spring brings back:
Lower things maintain their alternating turns.

### LIII.

->**A triple medicine, not of the common kind.**<-
The sharp **Green of the Sages** (a) <note>original: *Sophicum viride*. In alchemy, this often refers to "vitriol" or the "Green Lion," a powerful solvent used in the early stages of the Great Work.</note> gives the first: and gracious **Venus** <note>In alchemical shorthand, Venus represents the metal copper.</note> gives the second:

The second attracts the virtues of heaven, like a **magnet**:
for the rest, **cooking** <note>original: *coctio*. A technical term for the steady application of heat to a substance to mature or purify it.</note> alone is sufficient.
The third joins the powers of both heaven and earth:
By watering the sea-salt with the dew of heaven.

### LIV.

### The Spirit, the renewer of all things.
<note>original: *Spiritus omnium innovator.*</note>
He torments himself, he loathes himself, and he grows cold and stiff,
Who remains buried in the **old Adam** <note>original: *veteri Adam*. A theological concept referring to the unredeemed, sinful state of humanity inherited from the first man, Adam, which must be overcome for spiritual progress.</note>.
Truly, the **Holy Spirit** <note>original: *Pneuma sacrum*. *Pneuma* is the Greek word for "breath" or "spirit," used here to denote the divine life-force that brings about spiritual rebirth.</note> alone renews all things:
The closer you approach it, the more you are made new therefrom.
Do you wish to become a **Phoenix** <note>The mythical bird that burns to ashes and is reborn; in alchemy, it symbolizes the final stage of the Great Work—the achievement of the Philosopher's Stone and spiritual immortality.</note>? Lay aside your old life:
When the flesh is conquered, the soul’s new life is brought back.

---

### LV.

### The one necessary thing.
<note>original: *Unum necessarium*. A reference to Luke 10:42, where Jesus tells Martha that "only one thing is needed."</note>
**Martha** <note>In the Gospel of Luke, Martha represents the "active life" of chores and worldly duties, while her sister Mary represents the "contemplative life" of spiritual focus.</note>, attending to many things, found the **One** with difficulty:
But the **Sister** seeking the One, found all things in the **One**.

### LVI.

### The best knowledge.
<note>original: *Optima scientia*. This can also be translated as "The Highest Science."</note>
He shall know many profound things, who has known himself:
**Man** is an entire world, contained within a small body.
But this **Microcosm** <note>original: *microcosmus*. The philosophical concept that the human being is a "little world" reflecting the structure and laws of the "macrocosm" or the entire universe.</note> contains within it
An internal abyss of darkness and **Light** <note>original: *Lux*.</note>: who is able to penetrate it?
Reason is inadequate if it depends only on the stars <note>A critique of relying solely on astrology or external celestial influences; the author argues for a deeper, internal spiritual source of truth.</note>:
The **Mind** <note>original: *Mens*. In this philosophical context, *Mens* refers to the highest faculty of the soul, capable of divine intuition.</note> alone is able to approach the eternal Light.
Yet our mind will never comprehend that Light by **acting** <note>original: *agendo*. Referring to active, worldly effort or the exertion of the will.</note>,
But by **undergoing** <note>original: *patiendo*. From the Latin *pati*, meaning both "to suffer" and "to be passive/receptive." It suggests that divine knowledge is received as a gift rather than seized by force.</note>: hence the best art is to know how to **be receptive** <note>original: *scire pati*. Literally "to know how to suffer" or "to know how to endure." In this mystical context, it refers to the soul's ability to remain still and receive divine influence.</note>.

# Elegy

->On the subject matter and author of this book.<-

Away from here! Stand far off from these sacred inner chambers, you who are uninitiated:
->Here, the priest of the Cross tends to the secret mysteries of God.<-
<note>original Latin: *Mysta*. This term refers to an initiate or a priest who handles sacred mysteries. The poet is framing the reading of this book as a religious initiation.</note>
He bears sacred things, not to be looked upon by a wicked company,
->He bears sacred things, which are always to be revealed to the faithful.<-
You especially, who possess the breath of divine light,
->A spirit and a virtue that are not enemies to the Cross,<-

<note>original Latin: *animo linguisque fauete*. A classical Roman formula (faete linguis) used at the start of religious rituals to command a holy silence.</note>

->Guide our steps as our companion, and at last, with your golden<-
->staff, restore your people to the dwellings of joy.<-
->And him whom you add to the *twelve* with *Christ’s help*,<-
<note>original: "bis senis." Literally "twice six," referring to the company of the twelve apostles.</note>
->As a token of our shared struggle,<-
<note>original: "tessara militiae." A 'tessera' was a small tablet used by Roman soldiers as a password or sign of identity.</note>
->He is your follower, he is your priest, O nourishing Cross;<-
->Continue to protect him, for he has served you well.<-
->Take heart! As you usually do, my Friend: through insults<-
->and crosses<-
->The path to the peak of true honor is opened.<-
->May the supreme Leader and the creator of the Cross himself<-
->grant to me,<-
->That I may follow You under the cross with a<-
->courageous heart!<-

->C. G. K.<-

| Term | Translation | Explanation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **sarcina** | bundle / baggage | Often used to describe worldly cares or the "pack" a soldier carries. |
| **onus** | burden | A weight or responsibility. |
| **palma** | palm tree | A symbol of victory; here, it represents rising up despite pressure. |
| **murus ahenus** | bronze wall | A metaphor for an unbreakable, steadfast defense. |
| **clypeus** | shield | A large round shield, symbolizing divine protection. |
| **satanae** | of Satan | Referring to the adversary or the devil. |
| **tessara militiae** | military token | A sign or password identifying a fellow soldier in the spiritual war. |
| **crux alma** | nourishing Cross | 'Alma' implies the Cross provides life-giving sustenance to the soul. |
| **sacerdos** | priest | A person dedicated to sacred rites and service. |
| **honoris iter** | the path of honor | The journey toward spiritual glory, which the author notes is paved with trials. |

<summary>This page concludes an introductory elegy by refuting the idea that the Cross is a heavy burden, using the metaphor of a palm tree that grows stronger under weight. It ends with a personal dedication to a "priest" and a prayer for the courage to follow Christ's example of suffering.</summary>
